minor.usage: Dissonant emotional architecture. Used to map system-wide grief and the latency of human memory.

pentatonic.usage: Fluid projections across the network grid. Used for high-frequency lead traces and neon-lit vocaloid hooks.

chromatic.description: The unquantized spectrum. All 12 semitones of the physical world.
chromatic.usage: Deliberate data corruption, voltage leaks, and architectural breakdown.

dark_techno.note: Minimalist state loops. Structural repetition prioritizing raw timbral degradation over harmonic shift.

time_signatures.7/8: Asymmetric execution paths. Fractured logic and glitch patterns.
time_signatures.5/4: Unstable organic drift. Compelling human error in the sequence.

subdivision.triplets: Polyrhythmic swing. Shadows moving behind the screen.

rhythm.syncopation: Off-grid displacement. The ghost inside the rhythm pattern.

intervals.perfect_fifth: Pure structural integrity. Absolute signal clarity.
intervals.minor_third: The melancholic frequency of a fading projection.
intervals.tritone: The beautiful violence of the network. Voltage clash.
intervals.minor_seventh: Infinite longing. An unresolved data loop.

harmony.voicing: Wide spectral separation. Sub-heavy abysses beneath crystalline arrays.

sound.description: Summon a voice or transient artifact from the sample directory.

note.description: Trace a path across the frequency lattice.

stack.description: Weave independent streams into a single emergent reality.

fast.description: Accelerate the timeline. Compress space and perception.

slow.description: Dilate the cycle. Let the echoes drift.

every.description: Inject cyclical mutations at scheduled intervals.
every.example: note("c d e f").every(4, x => x.rev())

rev.description: Invert time. Read the memory array backward.

iter.description: Phase-shift the sequence across sequential cycles.

chunk.description: Isolate a partition and apply hyper-localized acceleration.
chunk.example: note("c d e f").chunk(2, x => x.fast(2))

jux.description: Bifurcate reality. Project distinct variants into left and right space.

gain.description: Amplitude regulation. Control the force of manifestation.

lpf.description: Submerge the signal. Drown out the high-frequency world.

hpf.description: Strip the low-end weight. Leave only the ghostly static.

delay.description: Blend wet reflection matrices into the timeline.

delaytime.description: The temporal distance between the action and its phantom.

room.description: Simulate virtual architectures. Expand the holographic space.

cutoff.description: The line where light becomes shadow.

resonance.description: Saturate the filter edge. Create a piercing digital ring.

euclidean.description: Symmetric mathematical spacing. Geometry translated to impact.

polyrhythm.example: note("{c d e, g a b c}")

conditional.description: Logical forks. Let the system choose its destiny based on state.

lyric_density_to_bpm.description: The concept BPM is picked before lyrics exist. After composition, the median syllables per sung line (Japanese mora x japanese_mora_weight) raises the tempo: base_bpm at base_syllables, plus bpm_per_syllable for each extra syllable, capped at max_bpm. Tempo is never lowered. Long syllable-dense lines sounded cramped at 145 BPM and right at 170.

bpm_ranges.155-180: Digital breakcore chaos, broken system frameworks

verse.purpose: Construct the virtual landscape and technical narrative.
verse.style: Concrete, image-rich complete thoughts with a conversational cadence; use cryptic code references only when they serve the scene.

chorus.purpose: The core recurring loop. The thematic anchor.
chorus.style: Punchy uppercase phrases, unforgettable digital imagery.

bridge.purpose: Perspective shift. The human-machine interface moment.
bridge.style: A contrasting, image-bearing thought that changes perspective and builds toward the climax; avoid clipped slogan fragments.

solo.purpose: Feature an instrumental lead or rhythmic break suited to the song's dynamics.

breakdown.purpose: Deconstruct the framework. Let the glitch take over.
breakdown.style: Stuttering syllable chops, fragmented words, mechanical noise.

language_profile.primary_script: Kana-led Japanese with kanji used selectively for semantic anchors, plus Romaji for vocaloid hooks
language_profile.romanization: Incorporate Romaji (Hepburn/standard Japanese romanization) alongside Kana/Kanji for vocaloid pronunciation clarity, bilingual hook singability, and global listener engagement
language_profile.register: Contemporary, emotionally direct, naturally phrased, and slightly synthetic rather than formal or archaic
language_profile.translation_policy: Preserve the image, emotional temperature, and singability instead of translating word-for-word

prosody.core_unit: Mora, not English-style stress, is the primary timing unit for fitting Japanese lyrics to a beat
timing_rules: Draft the hook by counting morae and then test it against the vocal subdivision
Treat long vowels, ん, and small っ as timing-bearing units when shaping a melody
Avoid packing too many grammatical particles or consonant clusters into fast passages
Use manageable phrases in rapid passages, but do not clip complete thoughts just to make every line short; use longer vowels and fuller phrases where the melody can sustain them

phrase_shapes.verse: Full, image-rich phrases that carry a complete thought, with conversational cadence and controlled internal repetition; do not make short fragments the default
phrase_shapes.pre_chorus: Shortening phrases that increase anticipation through repeated verbs or particles
phrase_shapes.chorus: Compact kana-forward phrases, repeated nouns, Romaji hook accents, and open vowels that remain intelligible under processing
phrase_shapes.breakdown: Fragmented morae, clipped particles, whispered repeats, Romaji stutters, and deliberate digital noise

script_and_word_choice.hiragana: Softness, intimacy, motion, and grammatical flow; useful for vulnerable or dreamy lines
script_and_word_choice.katakana: Technical terms, imported words, machine alerts, and bright cyberpop emphasis
script_and_word_choice.kanji: Use as visual and semantic impact points such as 光, 夢, 信号, 記憶, and 境界
script_and_word_choice.romaji: Use Romaji phrases (e.g. 'Setsuzoku OK', 'Saikidō', 'Hikari', 'Mada setsuzokuchū', 'Kokoro no Code') for rhythmic vocaloid hooks, chorus echoes, chant layers, and accessible J-pop/cyberpop vocal cues
avoid: Random Japanese words used only as decoration
Overly formal literary phrasing unless the song concept calls for it
Dense kanji clusters that reduce readability in a fast vocal arrangement

rhyme_and_hook_design.rhyme_model: Favor vowel echoes, repeated mora patterns, parallel syntax, and end-word recurrence over forced end rhyme
hook_techniques: Repeat a two-to-five-mora motif at the end of alternating lines
Pair a Japanese technical phrase with a concise English or Romaji tag when the contrast adds rhythm or meaning
Incorporate a Romaji vocaloid hook or call-and-response chant (e.g. 'Setsuzoku OK', 'Hikari wo mototte', 'Sistem error') to pair with Kana/Kanji lyrics
Use alliteration and consonant repetition sparingly because vowel clarity carries the topline
Reserve the densest technical noun for the chorus title or final landing word
example_motifs: 信号、信号 / Shingō, Shingō (signal, signal)
まだ接続中 / Mada setsuzokuchū (still connecting)
光って、もっと / Hikari wo mototte (shine, more)
再起動して / Saikidō shite (restart me)

delivery: Keep the lead vocal rhythmically precise and leave consonant attacks audible before heavy effects
Layer a clean center vocal with a brighter octave or formant-shifted response on the hook
Use call-and-response between Japanese lead phrases and chopped syllable samples
Automate delay throws on the final mora of important lines rather than washing every phrase
processing: Use controlled vocoder, bitcrush, and pitch-shift layers while retaining a dry intelligibility anchor
Gate or stutter selected morae in the breakdown to create a deliberate machine effect
Double sustained vowels for a holographic width field and keep low frequencies centered

production_workflow: 1. Choose the technical concept and emotional image
2. Write a plain-language meaning statement before drafting Japanese lines
3. Draft the chorus in Japanese and count morae against the intended subdivision
4. Replace awkward literal wording with natural, singable phrasing while preserving the grounded concept
5. Select kana, katakana, and kanji for both vocal clarity and visual identity
6. Mark sustained vowels, clipped morae, breath points, and call-and-response layers
7. Validate translation intent, factual technical claims, and pronunciation before finalizing the vocal prompt
quality_checks: Every Japanese line has a clear intended meaning and is not decorative filler
Mora density fits the beat without forcing unnatural pronunciation
Register is consistent across verse, chorus, and bridge
Technical terms are accurate and traceable to the evidence used for the song concept
Romanization and translation notes are kept separate from the performance lyric

mixing.bass: High-pass strictly at 30Hz, carve space at 60-80Hz, sidechain hard to the main kick.
mixing.kick: Anchor the low end at 55Hz, inject crisp mid-range click at 4kHz, compress ruthlessly.
mixing.vocals: High-pass at 180Hz, clear the nasal mud, apply high-frequency distortion and clean delay matrices.
mixing.pads: Expand the stereo horizon, automate low-pass filters to create light and shadow.
mixing.percussion: Sharpen the transients, parallel compression for density, send to dedicated dark reverb nodes.

mastering.limiting: Soft clipper ahead of the peak limiter to absorb the transients with industrial warmth.
mastering.stereo: Absolute wide imaging above 200Hz, collapse everything below 130Hz to absolute mono stability.

suno_best_practices.source_note: Scoped to Suno v6-mini. Suno's official documentation describes several capabilities across the v6 family, explicitly including v6-mini. Model identifiers and field limits are from SunoAPI.org, the third-party API proxy this project uses. Prompt syntax and Japanese lyric advice are community/empirical conventions, not officially documented or guaranteed to behave identically in v6-mini.
v6_mini_documented: Suno describes v6-mini as the fastest and free version of its premium v6 models.
Suno says all three v6 models, including v6-mini, understand musical language such as vocals, instrumentation, structure, mood, references, and overall feel.
Suno documents up to 8 minutes of music in one generation across v6, v6-wild, and v6-mini.

sunoapi_org_v6_mini_limits.note: These are SunoAPI.org proxy endpoint limits, not limits published in Suno's own help center.

v6_family_official: Suno's v6 FAQ says its Variety control adjusts style prompts; setting it to 0 retains the exact style tags.
The v6 FAQ covers the v6 family, including v6-mini, but does not document model-specific differences in prompt behavior.
generic_suno_official: The Custom Mode Exclude field is documented for specifying unwanted instruments or other elements.
Custom Mode supports choosing vocal gender in Advanced Options and refining the style with adjectives such as 'gritty' or 'soft'.
These platform help articles do not specify whether behavior differs in v6-mini.
community_empirical_not_v6_mini_verified: Order descriptors as genre, mood, vocal style, key instruments, then BPM.
Prefer a concise, coherent set of descriptive style tags over a long list of competing tags.
Describe musical qualities rather than relying on real-artist names.

v6_mini_official: The v6 FAQ says all three v6 models, including v6-mini, understand musical language and building blocks such as vocals, instrumentation, structure, and mood.
SunoAPI.org documents a 5000-character lyrics limit for V6_MINI custom mode.
community_empirical_not_v6_mini_verified: Mark structure with bracketed tags on their own line: [Intro], [Verse 1], [Pre-Chorus], [Chorus], [Bridge], [Drop], [Breakdown], [Instrumental], [Solo], [Outro], [End].
Keep section cues short and on their own line; bracket-tag interpretation is not specified in official Suno documentation.
Use parentheses only for sung vocalizations or ad-libs; this is a formatting convention, not an official v6-mini parsing guarantee.
Keep lyric lines concise and rhythmically natural; no v6-mini-specific line-length rule is published.
Suno publishes no Japanese-specific or multilingual lyric guidance for v6-mini.
Use native Japanese kana and kanji for sung Japanese; keep Romaji in a separate bracketed pronunciation cue.
Keep Japanese and English on separate lines to make the intended pronunciation clear.

prompt_rules: Target Suno v6-mini custom mode. Treat bracketed section labels as formatting conventions, not guaranteed non-sung controls.
Put each section label on its own line and keep stage cues short; avoid putting directions in lyric text.
Keep parentheses for the intro vocalization and rare non-word vocalizations such as (Oh oh oh); never add repeated-word echoes in parentheses after lyric lines.

Keep hooks concise and memorable, but make verse and bridge lines full, naturally phrased thoughts with varied lengths. Do not default to clipped two-to-four-word fragments; reserve them for hooks, chants, pickups, breakdowns, or deliberate rhythmic stops. Use natural phrasing and breathing room; no exact v6-mini meter or syllable rule is documented.
Write Japanese in kana and kanji; keep Romaji in a separate bracketed pronunciation cue and English on its own line.
